How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use

By lowob · 13 May 2026 · Updated 10 November 2026 · 4-minute read · Strategy / Customers

An ideal customer profile should tell sales whom to pursue, why a company fits, and when to move on. Broad descriptions rarely help.

An ideal customer profile, ICP, is a written description of the customer a company should pursue first: the one most likely to buy, most likely to succeed with the product, and most likely to stay. It is the practical output of positioning, and it is the document that keeps marketing and sales pointed at the same people.

Most ICPs are written once, put in a slide, and ignored, because they describe a customer so broadly that every prospect qualifies.

What an ICP contains

Firmographic or demographic facts. For business buyers: industry, size, geography, stage, structure. For consumers: age, situation, income band, location. These are the filters, and they are the least interesting part.

Situational triggers. What is happening to the customer that makes the problem urgent now: a new regulation, a product launch, a failed vendor, a new leader, a funding event, a growth spurt, a deadline. Triggers explain why two identical companies buy at different times, and they are what makes an ICP useful for outbound.

The buying committee. Who feels the problem, who approves the spend, who can block it, and who has to implement. For consumer products, who influences the decision.

Disqualifiers. The characteristics that predict a bad customer: too small to pay, a technical stack the product does not fit, a use case it does not serve, a regulatory position the company cannot support. The disqualifier list is usually more valuable than the qualifier list, because it stops the pipeline filling with deals that will not close or will churn.

Evidence. The customers this description was built from, and what happened to them.

ICP versus persona

An ICP describes the account or the customer: the company or person worth pursuing. A persona describes an individual within the buying process: their role, goals, fears, and how they evaluate. A company sells to an ICP and communicates with personas. Confusing the two produces marketing aimed at "the CFO" with no view on which CFOs, at which companies, in which situation.

How to build one from evidence

Start with the customers who bought fastest, paid the most, expanded, and stayed. Pull their characteristics, the trigger that made them buy, who was involved, and what they said the problem was. Do the same for customers who churned or deals that were lost, and record what distinguished them. The pattern across both sets is the ICP. The differences are the disqualifiers.

If the company has fewer than ten customers, the ICP is a hypothesis, and it should say so. Write it narrowly anyway; a narrow hypothesis can be tested, and a broad one cannot.

The mistakes that make it useless

Writing it broadly so nobody is excluded. Building it from who the company wishes it sold to rather than who actually bought. Leaving out triggers, so it cannot inform timing. Leaving out disqualifiers, so it cannot inform saying no. Writing it once and never revising it as the customer base changes.

How to tell whether it is working

Sales can disqualify a lead in one call using shared criteria. Marketing can describe the audience for a channel test in the ICP's terms. Outbound lists are built from the triggers, not from a title search. And the customers acquired this quarter look more like the profile than the ones acquired last quarter.

An ICP that does those four things is a working document. One that does not is a slide.

lowob takeaways

  • Use real customer outcomes and buying signals to define fit.
  • Include reasons to disqualify an account.
  • Check that marketing and sales use the same criteria.
